planting.note: Set container plants in full sun to light shade and average, well-drained soil in spring or fall; space about 2-3 feet apart for a seamless low hedge or border planting.

directions: Little Bonnie is a compact dwarf spirea bred for Southern heat tolerance, holding its blue-green summer foliage without scorching and turning gold in autumn. Clusters of lavender-pink flowers open in late spring to early summer and draw pollinators readily; shearing off spent blooms often triggers a second flush. Site it in full sun to light shade with average, well-drained soil, where its dense, naturally rounded habit suits foundation plantings, borders, and containers. It is largely trouble-free, needing only a late-winter to early-spring prune to refresh its shape before new growth emerges.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection official site

planting.note: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil, including alkaline sites, after the chance of hard frost has passed; it blooms on new wood, so prune in late winter or early spring if shaping is needed.

directions: Featherman is a sterile chastetree selected for an unusually dense, upright, narrow-leaved silhouette rather than for showy bloom, though pale purple flower spikes still rise above the foliage in late spring and summer. Its finely cut, feather-like leaves give the plant a soft, almost conifer-like texture that sets it apart from typical open-branched Vitex. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil, where it tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline ground with ease. In the colder end of its range it may die back to the ground over winter, which simply resets the plant for another full season of new-wood bloom.

planting.note: Set plants in full sun in any well-drained soil, including sandy or chalky ground, once the danger of frost has passed; it is self-fertile, so a single plant will set fruit without a second cultivar nearby.

directions: Candybox is a compact, self-fruiting selection of Chilean guava bred for dense, boxwood-like branching that takes well to shearing into hedges or rounded forms. Small pink spring flowers need no second plant to set fruit, and the shiny dark green leaves give way in fall to red berries often described as tasting like candy. It thrives in full sun across a wide range of soil types, including sandy or chalky ground, and tolerates both drought and some salt exposure once established. Use it as a low hedge, edging, or container specimen in warm-winter gardens where traditional boxwood struggles with summer heat.
